hints: Remember disproportionation means the same element is both oxidised and reduced in one reaction, so track oxidation numbers of nitrogen.
In $\text{NO}_2$, nitrogen is +4, while in $\text{HNO}_3$ it is +5 and in $\text{HNO}_2$ it is +3, so one has gone up and one has gone down.
Check the other equations to confirm nitrogen keeps the same oxidation number or different elements change, leaving only one where nitrogen splits both ways.
walkthrough:
**Recall what disproportionation means**

Think of it as one element doing two opposite jobs at once. The same element is oxidised (oxidation number increases) and also reduced (oxidation number decreases).

Rule to use:
$$\text{disproportionation = same element} \rightarrow \text{higher oxidation state + lower oxidation state}$$

**Assign oxidation numbers to nitrogen**

This is the quickest way to see what is happening. Remember O is -1 in peroxides, -2 normally, H is +1, and the sum equals the charge.

Key values:
$$\text{N in N}_2 = 0, \quad \text{N in NH}_3 \text{ and } \text{NH}_4^+ = -3, \quad \text{N in NO}_2 = +4, \quad \text{N in HNO}_2 = +3, \quad \text{N in HNO}_3 \text{ and NO}_3^- = +5$$

**Test option D**

In $2\text{NO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{HNO}_3 + \text{HNO}_2$, nitrogen starts at +4 in both $\text{NO}_2$ molecules. One ends at +5, so oxidised, and the other ends at +3, so reduced.

Change shown:
$$+4 \rightarrow +5 \text{ (oxidation) and } +4 \rightarrow +3 \text{ (reduction)}$$

**Confirm the others are not disproportionation**

In A, N stays at +5 throughout. In C, N stays at -3 throughout. In B, N goes $0 \rightarrow -3$ and H goes $0 \rightarrow +1$, so different elements are oxidised and reduced. That is normal redox, not disproportionation.

options.A: This is an acid plus carbonate reaction to give a salt, $\text{CO}_2$ and water. Nitrogen stays at +5 in $\text{HNO}_3$ and in $\text{Ca(NO}_3)_2$, and carbon stays at +4, so no oxidation or reduction occurs.
options.B: This is redox but not disproportionation. Nitrogen is reduced from 0 in $\text{N}_2$ to -3 in $\text{NH}_3$, while hydrogen is oxidised from 0 in $\text{H}_2$ to +1 in $\text{NH}_3$. Different elements change, so it fails the same-element test.
options.C: This is an acid-base reaction between ammonium salt and alkali to release ammonia. Nitrogen remains -3 in $\text{NH}_4^+$ and in $\text{NH}_3$, so there is no change in oxidation number at all.
options.D: This is correct because nitrogen in $\text{NO}_2$ at +4 splits two ways. One N is oxidised to +5 in $\text{HNO}_3$ and the other N is reduced to +3 in $\text{HNO}_2$. Same element both oxidised and reduced, the definition of disproportionation.
